messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] [g.part2] and [g.part3]: wrongly detected inactivity bouts
messages.body_plain:
Hi Luca,

I just had a look.

GGIR detects 26.6% of your recording as signal clipping, indicating
that the acceleration signal was near the edge of the dynamic range
for a substantial amount of time. I rarely see this, and it can
indicate that there is something wrong with the accelerometer.

Next, GGIR imputes those clipping periods, and this is why the
sustained inactivity bout (sleep) classifications does not match the
pattern in the raw signal. GGIR is using the impute values and not the
raw values. If I remember correctly this is not something you can
easily turn off as a user.

To get to the cause of the problem:
1. Are you using the Axivity with a dynamic range setting different than 8g?
2. Do you spot anything in the acceleration signal within OMGui that
indicates extreme values?
3. Have you tried processing the cwa files as well as the
wav-converted files? It would be interesting to see whether the
problem is consistent between file formats.

Also I notice that you processed the data with anglethreshold = 1,
rahter than 5, but I do not think that is the problem.

Best wishes,
Vincent

messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] What is the difference between mvpathreshold in part2 and threshold.vig in part5?
messages.subject_clean: [GGIR] What is the difference between mvpathreshold in part2 and threshold.vig in part5?
messages.body_plain:
Good question,
I implemented it in this way because I assumed that Physical activity
researchers are not interested in the distinction between non-bouted
and bouted vigorous physical activity.
Part 5 calculated time spent in vigorous activity, but when it comes
to bouted behavior it only looks at bouted mvpa, light and inactiivty
(sedentary).

Note that argument mvpathreshold is only used in part 2, because that
is how GGIR evolved.
Later when I added part 5 I created argument threshold.mod, which is
used in part5 for calculating timespent in MVPA.

ilevels does not have default values, because it is not calculated by default.

 Best, Vincent

messages.body_plain:
Did you try starting again with a clean output folder and/or setting
overwrite = TRUE?
Changing input arguments mid-way and analysis can sometimes confuse GGIR.
Also, the errors seems related to your sleeplog. Try loading your
sleeplog files with function g.loadlog only and if that doesn't work
then it indicates that something is wrong with your sleeplog file.
Vincent

messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] Re: CSV input issues
messages.body_plain:
HI Scott,
GGIR can handle Axivity csv files based on one specific way of
exporting the ata, sorry it looks like this is not clearly documented
yet.

In OMGui, do:
- Export to raw csv
- Unit gravity
- Formatted (Y-M-D h:m:s.f)

You should then get a csv file without header columns, which GGIR is
able to handle.
Other Axivity csv export formats have not been implemented yet... I am
happy to work on that as part of a paid consultancy though.

Best, Vincent

messages.subject: Time missing from data sets
messages.body_plain:
I am currently analysing my ActiGraph RAW data files in R, using the GGIR package and have come across a problem and wondered if you would be able to advise me on how to correct this or why this occurs.

I have managed to run my data files through R and have CSV files outputs. However, the CSV files have the first 10 minutes of initialised time removed (this time is sometimes longer in other data files). For example, my ActiLife RAW data file starts at 13:30:00 but the CSV file from GGIR starts at 13:40:00. Is there any way to correct this or can you please advise me why this happens?

Thank you for your time and I look forward to hearing from you
Ruth Brady

messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] Time missing from data sets
messages.body_plain:
GGIR always outputs the epochs from the first integer number windows used for the non-wear detection.
So, if you set it at 600 seconds (second value in argument windowsizes) then your output will start at 0, 10, 20, 30, 40, or 50 minutes past the hour. It might be that starting the measurement at 13:30 still rounds it off to 13:40. I did this to be able to standardise the timing of epochs, which would ease merging it with other time series, and avoids confusion about the hour or day an epoch belongs to.
In short, your timestamps are not incorrect, the code simply ignores the first bit of data. Something similar happens at the very end of the measurement.
Cheers, Vincent

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am happy to tell you about the "International Workshop: a focus on statistical methods to analyse accelerometer-measured physical activity" (AIW2019) that we are going to host in Granada (Spain), the October 21st, 2019. Top experts will talk about compositional data analysis, multivariate pattern analysis and machine learning, the workshop will also include a hands-on session on accelerometer data processing with GGIR. More info and registrations here --> https://www.granadacongresos.com/aiw2019

THE WORKSHOP
Objective instruments to measure physical activity are evolving at a drastic velocity. Recent developments have allowed to classify the accelerations produced by the human body as sleep, sedentary or physical activity time with a gradient of intensities. These categories of physical behaviour coexist in the 24 hours of the day with inter-relationships that classical statistical methods fail to consider. Researchers from all around the world are investigating how to overcome this limitation at analysing physical activity temporal series by using new statistical approaches such as isotemporal substitution models, compositional data analysis, multivariate pattern analysis with partial least squares regression and/or even machine learning algorithms.

The present international workshop has been organized with the purpose of gathering together top experts from different countries in the abovementioned approaches to analyse physical activity data. This meeting will bring together different point of views on the state-of-the-art of physical activity data analysis, which will encourage interesting debates and, hopefully, will end up with practical recommendations on how to keep advancing to appropriately analyse physical activity data.

We welcome all people interested in the topic to join us in Granada (Spain). All attendees will have the chance to send their abstract and present their studies as oral communications or posters during the workshop.

I am happy to answer your related questions here or by email (jai...@ugr.es). Hope to see you in Granada!

Best,
Jairo

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jairo,

thanks a lot for organizing that workshop, it sounds fantastic.
What kind of abstracts are you expecting? Any studies including activity data analyses or evaluations of different approaches with regard to statistics?

Best regards,
David

Am Sonntag, 23. Juni 2019 11:27:39 UTC+2 schrieb Jairo Hidalgo Migueles:
> Dear all,
>
> I am happy to tell you about the "International Workshop: a focus on statistical methods to analyse accelerometer-measured physical activity" (AIW2019) that we are going to host in Granada (Spain), the October 21st, 2019. Top experts will talk about compositional data analysis, multivariate pattern analysis and machine learning, the workshop will also include a hands-on session on accelerometer data processing with GGIR. More info and registrations here --> https://www.granadacongresos.com/aiw2019
>
> THE WORKSHOP
> Objective instruments to measure physical activity are evolving at a drastic velocity. Recent developments have allowed to classify the accelerations produced by the human body as sleep, sedentary or physical activity time with a gradient of intensities. These categories of physical behaviour coexist in the 24 hours of the day with inter-relationships that classical statistical methods fail to consider. Researchers from all around the world are investigating how to overcome this limitation at analysing physical activity temporal series by using new statistical approaches such as isotemporal substitution models, compositional data analysis, multivariate pattern analysis with partial least squares regression and/or even machine learning algorithms.
>
> The present international workshop has been organized with the purpose of gathering together top experts from different countries in the abovementioned approaches to analyse physical activity data. This meeting will bring together different point of views on the state-of-the-art of physical activity data analysis, which will encourage interesting debates and, hopefully, will end up with practical recommendations on how to keep advancing to appropriately analyse physical activity data.
>
> We welcome all people interested in the topic to join us in Granada (Spain). All attendees will have the chance to send their abstract and present their studies as oral communications or posters during the workshop.
>
> I am happy to answer your related questions here or by email (jai...@ugr.es). Hope to see you in Granada!
>
> Best,
> Jairo
